summary.text: Lucas congruences split the defining sums at \(p\), making the two parts cancel for \(p\le n\le2p-2\); at \(n=p-1\), they give \(a(p-1)=1\), while divisibility of central binomial coefficients leaves only the middle term for \(c\), giving \(c(p-1)=(-1)^{(p-1)/2}\) modulo \(p\). Reversing the columns of each Hankel matrix then makes it triangular with constant diagonal \(f(p-1)\); the reversal has sign \((-1)^{(p-1)/2}\), and \(f(p-1)^p=f(p-1)\) modulo \(p\), yielding the two determinants.

full_proof.text:
Let
\[
a(n)=\sum_{k=0}^{n}(-1)^k\binom nk^4
\]
and
\[
c(n)=\sum_{k=0}^{n}(-1)^k\binom nk^2
       \binom{2k}{k}\binom{2(n-k)}{n-k}.
\]
Fix an odd prime \(p\), and put
\[
h=\frac{p-1}{2}.
\]
Thus \(p=2h+1\). All congruences below are modulo \(p\), or equivalently are identities in the field \(\mathbb F_p\).

We first establish the binomial-coefficient congruences that will be used repeatedly.

## 1. A one-step Lucas congruence

For arbitrary nonnegative integers \(N,K\), write
\[
N=qp+r,\qquad K=sp+t,
\]
where \(0\le r,t<p\). Then
\[
\binom NK\equiv \binom rt\binom qs\pmod p. \tag{1}
\]
Indeed, in \(\mathbb F_p[X]\), the binomial theorem gives
\[
(1+X)^p\equiv 1+X^p.
\]
Consequently,
\[
(1+X)^N=(1+X)^{qp+r}
 \equiv (1+X^p)^q(1+X)^r.
\]
The coefficient of \(X^{sp+t}\) on the right is
\(\binom qs\binom rt\): because \((1+X^p)^q\) contains only powers divisible by \(p\), while \((1+X)^r\) has degree less than \(p\), there is only one possible way to obtain exponent \(sp+t\). Comparing coefficients proves (1).

Several special cases will be needed.

### 1.1. The row immediately preceding \(p\)

For \(0\le k<p\),
\[
\binom{p-1}{k}\equiv(-1)^k. \tag{2}
\]
One direct proof is
\[
\binom{p-1}{k}
 =\frac{(p-1)(p-2)\cdots(p-k)}{k!}
 \equiv\frac{(-1)(-2)\cdots(-k)}{k!}=(-1)^k.
\]
All the factors in \(k!\) are invertible modulo \(p\), since \(k<p\).

### 1.2. A row of the form \(p+r\)

If \(0\le r<p\) and \(0\le k<2p\), formula (1) gives
\[
\binom{p+r}{k}\equiv
\begin{cases}
\binom rk,&0\le k<p,\\[2mm]
\binom r{k-p},&p\le k<2p.
\end{cases} \tag{3}
\]
Here the quotient digits of \(p+r\) are \(1,r\); the quotient digit of \(k\) is respectively \(0\) or \(1\).

### 1.3. Central binomial coefficients

If \(0\le m<p\) and \(2m\ge p\), then
\[
\binom{2m}{m}\equiv0. \tag{4}
\]
To see this, write \(2m=p+(2m-p)\). The low base-\(p\) digit of the top is \(2m-p\), which is strictly less than \(m\), whereas \(m<p\). Formula (1) therefore contains the factor
\(\binom{2m-p}{m}=0\).

We will also use, for every \(0\le m<p\),
\[
\binom{2p+2m}{p+m}\equiv 2\binom{2m}{m}. \tag{5}
\]
There are two cases. If \(2m<p\), formula (1) gives
\[
\binom{2p+2m}{p+m}
 \equiv \binom{2m}{m}\binom21
 =2\binom{2m}{m}.
\]
If \(2m\ge p\), write \(2m=p+(2m-p)\). The low digit \(2m-p\) is less than \(m\), so the left side is zero by (1). The central coefficient on the right is also zero by (4). Thus (5) holds in both cases.

## 2. The values of \(a(n)\) needed for the determinant

We prove
\[
a(p-1)\equiv1, \tag{6}
\]
and
\[
a(n)\equiv0\qquad(p\le n\le2p-2). \tag{7}
\]

For (6), use (2):
\[
\begin{aligned}
a(p-1)
&=\sum_{k=0}^{p-1}(-1)^k\binom{p-1}{k}^4\\
&\equiv\sum_{k=0}^{p-1}(-1)^k\bigl((-1)^k\bigr)^4
 =\sum_{k=0}^{p-1}(-1)^k.
\end{aligned}
\]
Because \(p\) is odd, the first \(p-1\) terms cancel in adjacent pairs and the last term, with even exponent \(p-1\), is \(1\). Hence (6).

Now suppose \(p\le n\le2p-2\), and write
\[
n=p+r,
\]
where \(0\le r\le p-2\). Split the defining sum for \(a(p+r)\) into the ranges \(0\le k<p\) and \(p\le k\le p+r\).

In the first range, (3) gives
\(\binom{p+r}{k}\equiv\binom rk\). For \(k>r\), this is zero. Therefore this part of the sum is
\[
\sum_{k=0}^{p-1}(-1)^k\binom{p+r}{k}^4
 \equiv \sum_{k=0}^{r}(-1)^k\binom rk^4
 =a(r). \tag{8}
\]

In the second range, write \(k=p+x\), where \(0\le x\le r\). By (3),
\[
\binom{p+r}{p+x}\equiv\binom rx.
\]
Since \(p\) is odd,
\[
(-1)^{p+x}=-(-1)^x.
\]
Thus the second part is
\[
\sum_{x=0}^{r}(-1)^{p+x}\binom{p+r}{p+x}^4
 \equiv-\sum_{x=0}^{r}(-1)^x\binom rx^4
 =-a(r). \tag{9}
\]
The two parts (8) and (9) cancel, proving (7).

## 3. The values of \(c(n)\) needed for the determinant

We next prove
\[
c(p-1)\equiv(-1)^h, \tag{10}
\]
and
\[
c(n)\equiv0\qquad(p\le n\le2p-2). \tag{11}
\]

### 3.1. Evaluation of \(c(p-1)\)

By (2), for every \(0\le k<p\),
\[
\binom{p-1}{k}^2\equiv \bigl((-1)^k\bigr)^2=1.
\]
Hence
\[
c(p-1)\equiv
\sum_{k=0}^{p-1}(-1)^k
 \binom{2k}{k}
 \binom{2(p-1-k)}{p-1-k}. \tag{12}
\]
We show that every summand except the one with \(k=h\) vanishes.

If \(k<h\), put \(m=p-1-k=2h-k\). Then \(m<p\), and because \(k<h\),
\[
2m=2(p-1-k)\ge p.
\]
Therefore the second central binomial coefficient in (12) vanishes by (4).

If \(k>h\), then \(k<p\) and
\[
2k\ge p,
\]
so the first central binomial coefficient vanishes by (4).

Thus only \(k=h\) remains. Since \(2h=p-1\), both central coefficients in that summand are \(\binom{p-1}{h}\). By (2),
\[
\binom{p-1}{h}\equiv(-1)^h.
\]
Their product is therefore \(1\), and the remaining sign is \((-1)^h\). This proves (10).

### 3.2. Vanishing of \(c(n)\) on the upper range

Let \(n=p+r\), where \(0\le r\le p-2\). Split the sum defining \(c(p+r)\) at \(p\).

First consider \(0\le k<p\). Formula (3) gives
\[
\binom{p+r}{k}\equiv\binom rk,
\]
so terms with \(k>r\) vanish. For \(0\le k\le r\), we have
\[
p+r-k=p+(r-k).
\]
Using (5) with \(m=r-k<p\),
\[
\binom{2(p+r-k)}{p+r-k}
=\binom{2p+2(r-k)}{p+(r-k)}
\equiv2\binom{2(r-k)}{r-k}.
\]
It follows that the entire part with \(k<p\) is
\[
\begin{aligned}
&\sum_{k=0}^{p-1}(-1)^k\binom{p+r}{k}^2
 \binom{2k}{k}\binom{2(p+r-k)}{p+r-k}\\
&\qquad\equiv
2\sum_{k=0}^{r}(-1)^k\binom rk^2
 \binom{2k}{k}\binom{2(r-k)}{r-k}
=2c(r). \tag{13}
\end{aligned}
\]

For the remaining terms write \(k=p+x\), with \(0\le x\le r\). Then (3) gives
\[
\binom{p+r}{p+x}\equiv\binom rx,
\]
and (5) gives
\[
\binom{2(p+x)}{p+x}\equiv2\binom{2x}{x}.
\]
Also,
\[
p+r-(p+x)=r-x
\]
and, because \(p\) is odd,
\[
(-1)^{p+x}=-(-1)^x.
\]
Consequently this second part equals
\[
\begin{aligned}
&\sum_{x=0}^{r}(-1)^{p+x}\binom{p+r}{p+x}^2
 \binom{2(p+x)}{p+x}\binom{2(r-x)}{r-x}\\
&\qquad\equiv
-2\sum_{x=0}^{r}(-1)^x\binom rx^2
 \binom{2x}{x}\binom{2(r-x)}{r-x}
=-2c(r). \tag{14}
\end{aligned}
\]
The two contributions (13) and (14) cancel. This proves (11).

## 4. A determinant lemma for a Hankel matrix with an upper vanishing range

Let \(f\colon\mathbb N\to\mathbb Z\) be any sequence such that
\[
f(n)\equiv0\qquad(p\le n\le2p-2). \tag{15}
\]
Form the \(p\times p\) Hankel matrix
\[
M=(f(i+j))_{0\le i,j<p}.
\]
We claim that
\[
\det M\equiv(-1)^h f(p-1). \tag{16}
\]

Reverse the order of the columns of \(M\). The resulting matrix \(B\) has entries
\[
B_{ij}=f\bigl(i+(p-1-j)\bigr),
\qquad 0\le i,j<p.
\]
If \(i>j\), then
\[
i+p-1-j\ge p.
\]
Also, since both \(i\) and \(p-1-j\) are at most \(p-1\),
\[
i+p-1-j\le2p-2.
\]
Thus (15) implies \(B_{ij}\equiv0\) whenever \(i>j\). Hence \(B\) is upper triangular modulo \(p\).

On its diagonal,
\[
B_{ii}=f(i+p-1-i)=f(p-1).
\]
Therefore
\[
\det B\equiv f(p-1)^p. \tag{17}
\]
In \(\mathbb F_p\), every element \(x\) satisfies \(x^p=x\): this is Fermat's theorem for nonzero \(x\), and is immediate for \(x=0\). Thus (17) becomes
\[
\det B\equiv f(p-1). \tag{18}
\]

It remains to account for the sign of the reversal permutation. Reversing \(p\) objects has
\[
0+1+\cdots+(p-1)=\frac{p(p-1)}2=ph
\]
inversions, so its sign is
\[
(-1)^{ph}=(-1)^h,
\]
because \(p\) is odd. Permuting the columns by this reversal multiplies the determinant by its sign. Therefore
\[
\det B=(-1)^h\det M.
\]
The sign \((-1)^h\) is its own inverse, and hence
\[
\det M=(-1)^h\det B.
\]
Combining this with (18) proves (16).

## 5. Application to the two sequences

For the first matrix
\[
A=(a(i+j))_{0\le i,j<p},
\]
the vanishing statement (7) permits us to apply (16) with \(f=a\). Using (6), we obtain
\[
\det A\equiv(-1)^h a(p-1)
\equiv(-1)^h.
\]
Since \(h=(p-1)/2\), this is exactly
\[
\boxed{\det(a(i+j))_{0\le i,j<p}\equiv(-1)^{(p-1)/2}\pmod p}.
\]

For the second matrix
\[
C=(c(i+j))_{0\le i,j<p},
\]
the vanishing statement (11) and the determinant formula (16), together with (10), give
\[
\det C\equiv(-1)^h c(p-1)
\equiv(-1)^h(-1)^h
=(-1)^{2h}=1.
\]
Therefore
\[
\boxed{\det(c(i+j))_{0\le i,j<p}\equiv1\pmod p}.
\]

Both asserted determinant congruences follow.
